# The Future of Work, Designed Lightly: A Framework of Few Rules and Strong Principles

Offered for the group's consideration, in the spirit of the previous proposal: we begin with a stance rather than a policy, because a policy ages but a stance adapts. One quiet observation frames everything below — most global work policies fail not because they are wrong, but because they are *uniform*. They encode one country's norms (usually the headquarters country's) and call the result "global." Perhaps the more useful question is not *"how many days in the office?"* but *"what is each place, each hour, and each tool actually good at — and for whom?"*

A second observation, offered with equal care: most future-of-work documents fail in a quieter way. They are written about knowledge workers while speaking of "all employees." We have tried not to make that mistake here.

## 1. The Design Stance: Minimum Viable Policy

We would gently propose four commitments before any specifics:

- **Work is an activity, not a location** — though some activities *have* a location. Design around what people *do* — focus, create, mentor, belong, decide, make, move, serve — and let place follow purpose.
- **Principles are global; practices are local; choices are personal.** The center holds very little, firmly. Everything else is delegated downward.
- **Trust is the default; verification is the exception.** Policies written for the 3% who might abuse them tax the 97% who won't. We suggest pricing that tax honestly.
- **Every policy carries an owner and an expiry date.** Rules should earn their renewal with evidence, the way pilots do. Few things calcify faster than a temporary arrangement.

A question worth holding throughout: *which of our current rules exist because they serve people — and which because they once served a building?*

## 2. Whom This Framework Serves: Three Populations, One Promise

The request before us concerns *all* employees worldwide, so we would propose naming the populations plainly rather than letting one stand silently for the whole:

| Population | Examples | What flexibility can honestly mean |
|---|---|---|
| **Location-flexible** | Most office and knowledge roles | The full remote/hybrid spectrum this framework describes |
| **Location-bound** | Manufacturing, labs, retail, logistics, facilities, field operations | Flexibility of *time and control*: schedules published reliably ahead; self-service shift swapping; compressed patterns (4×10, nine-day fortnights) where the work allows; flexitime bands; part-time and job-share paths; cross-training for variety |
| **Place-anchored but mobile** | Field service, sales, technicians | Flexibility of *route and rhythm*: sensible territory design, administrative time done remotely, dispatch-from-home where feasible |

The governing principle might be called **parity of regard**: flexibility differs in *form* across these populations, but never in *dignity*. If desk-based colleagues gain autonomy while site-based colleagues gain only monitoring, we will have built precisely the two-tier workforce this framework warns against — along role lines rather than remote/office lines. Schedule unpredictability is among the most documented drivers of frontline attrition, and field experiments in retail associate stable, predictable scheduling with measurable gains in both retention and sales. Predictability is among the cheapest flexibility we can offer, and among the most valued.

We would therefore suggest that every team charter — including plant, store, and depot charters — be required to answer one question honestly: *what does flexibility mean here?* And that the answer be co-designed with the people it affects, not presented to them.

## 3. The Framework: One Spine, Many Rhythms

A four-layer model, with decision rights placed as low as they can responsibly sit:

| Layer | What it decides | Who decides | How much it contains |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — The Spine** (global guardrails) | Security & data residency; legal compliance; **work authorization** (employees may work only where they hold the legal right to work — cross-border days capped, pre-approved, and tracked with consent); **duty of care** (responsibility for health, safety, ergonomics, and well-being follows the employee to wherever work happens); the equity principle (flexibility never penalizes); a handful of in-person "moments that matter" (onboarding, kickoffs, periodic gatherings) | Global leadership + legal | As little as possible — this is the one place where "must" is honest |
| **1 — Country addenda** | Local labor law, works-council agreements, telework entitlements, holiday & rest rhythms, infrastructure support | Country HR/legal, co-designed with local employees | One page per country, reviewed annually |
| **2 — Team charters** | Core overlap hours, response-time expectations, meeting norms, which rituals are in person, focus-time blocks — and, for location-bound teams, scheduling predictability, swap protocols, and pattern options | Each team, facilitated, reviewed quarterly | One page per team, with a sunset clause |
| **3 — Individual flexibility** | Location and hours within the charter; caregiving needs; "work-from-elsewhere" days within tax- and immigration-safe limits | The individual | Bounded only by the charter above it |

The intent is that an employee in São Paulo and one in Stockholm share the same *spine* but live in genuinely different, locally coherent rhythms — and that a colleague on a production line and one in a product team experience the same *regard*, expressed in forms that fit their work.

## 4. Cultural Calibration: The Quiet Variable

Culture rarely appears in policy documents, yet it silently determines whether a policy lands. Dimensions worth mapping before finalizing anything — sketched as direction only, with the humble request that local counsel and local colleagues verify each line:

| Dimension | How it varies | Design implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Communication context** | Low-context cultures (Germany, Nordics, US) often thrive on written async; high-context cultures (Japan, Korea, Gulf, much of LatAm) carry meaning in tone, pause, and relationship | Offer *rich* async — voice notes, short video — alongside text; protect synchronous rituals where relationship is the medium |
| **Power distance** | Where hierarchy is strong, an "optional" office day is read as "expected" if leaders attend | Permission must be made *legible* — leaders model flexibility explicitly, or the policy is fiction |
| **Uncertainty avoidance** | Some cultures find open-ended flexibility stressful rather than liberating | Provide clear defaults and norms to opt *out* of, rather than blank choice to opt into |
| **Home infrastructure** | Urban density (Tokyo, Mumbai, Manila) can mean small, multigenerational homes; bandwidth and power reliability vary | Coworking stipends; an office-first option without stigma; low-bandwidth modes for all tools |
| **Regulatory texture** | France, Spain, and Portugal have established disconnection rights in varying forms; Belgium requires private employers with 20+ staff to *negotiate* disconnection arrangements through collective agreement (a statutory individual right currently covers federal public servants). Germany's works councils hold co-determination over working time and monitoring. In the Netherlands, location requests are difficult for employers to refuse without substantial business grounds under the Flexible Working Act — though the broader "Work Where You Want" bill was declined by the Senate in 2023, so the landscape is permissive rather than absolute. Mexico's NOM-037 obliges employers to fund telework ergonomics and connectivity | Country addenda drafted *with* local counsel and employee representatives — in much of Europe, consultation is not a courtesy but a requirement, and early engagement is wise regardless |
| **Calendar & rhythm** | Ramadan, festival seasons, differing weekends, harvest and fiscal cycles | Local calendars shape collaboration windows; no global meeting is ever truly "neutral" |

A question the group may wish to sit with: *whose definition of "professional" is doing the silent work inside our current policies?*

## 5. Place: The Office Must Earn the Commute

- **Redesign for purpose, not presence.** Offices become destinations for what they do best — collaborative creation, mentoring, client hosting, belonging — rather than rows of desks for work better done elsewhere. Quiet zones, bookable project rooms, and event-capable space; privacy and noise norms tuned locally.
- **Hub-and-spoke with a third option.** Regional hubs, smaller spokes, and coworking passes for those far from either — so "office access" isn't a proxy for "lives near headquarters."
- **For location-bound colleagues, the site *is* the workplace experience.** The same design respect applies: dignified rest and prayer spaces, reliable transport and parking, schedule visibility without having to ask a supervisor, decent shift-handover areas. These are inexpensive signals of regard, and their absence is expensive.
- **Fund gathering from footprint savings.** A modest, deliberate rhythm — anchor weeks, team offsites, in-person onboarding — typically costs a fraction of the real estate it replaces and does more for culture than any tool (see Section 10).
- **Protect the apprenticeship layer.** Early-career employees learn by osmosis; fully remote setups can become mentorship deserts. We would suggest in-person-anchored first 90 days and structured apprenticeship pods — quietly noting that this cohort rarely appears in policy debates, yet absorbs their costs.

## 6. Time: Async by Default, Synchronous by Intention

- **Documentation as the single source of truth** — decisions written down, findable, translated where needed. This also quietly favors non-native speakers, who often read faster than they parse rapid speech.
- **Time-zone fairness as a tracked practice.** Rotate early/late meetings so the same region doesn't permanently carry the "time-zone debt"; define narrow overlap windows; use follow-the-sun handoffs where work allows.
- **Meeting hygiene with teeth:** agendas, recordings, default 25/50 minutes, team-chosen meeting-free blocks.
- **For shift-based teams, time design is the policy:** rosters published at least two to four weeks ahead; changes by consent or by premium; swap requests answerable in hours, not days.
- **Honor disconnection normatively, not just legally.** After-hours messaging norms set by charter; leaders measured on their teams' rest, not just their output.
- **One caveat, offered humbly:** async-first is itself a culturally loaded preference. In relationship-first markets, a well-timed five-minute call can do what ten messages cannot. The charter, not the framework, should decide the blend.

## 7. Tools: The Digital Workplace as Infrastructure

Principles rather than a shopping list: interoperability; low-bandwidth and mobile-first modes; accessibility; availability by country (the stack must work where people are — including behind firewalls, which may mean sanctioned local equivalents); data residency respected.

On measurement, we would suggest restraint made explicit: **measure outcomes, not keystrokes — and measure patterns only in aggregate.** Any work-pattern data (meeting load, focus time, after-hours activity) is reported at team level or above, anonymized, with a minimum group size; no individual dashboards without the individual's own consent and, where applicable, works-council agreement. Surveillance tooling tends to purchase a small amount of visibility at a large cost in trust — and in several jurisdictions it requires co-determination anyway. The measurement standard in Section 12 follows this principle exactly, so that our data practices never contradict our stated stance.

## 8. Equity: Avoiding the Two-Tier Workforce — on Two Axes

The two-tier risk runs along *two* axes: remote versus on-site, and desk versus non-desk. Both deserve direct audit.

- **Audit proximity bias directly.** Compare promotion and performance ratings between remote and on-site employees — and between location-flexible and location-bound populations — quarterly; publish the ratios internally. What gets measured gets managed.
- **Parity of investment:** home-office and coworking stipends, ergonomic support, and equal access to learning, regardless of where the desk sits — or whether there is a desk at all.

**On pay, we would propose a genuine decision rather than a deferral.** Each philosophy tells a different fairness story, and the differences are not small:

| Philosophy | The story it tells | What it offers | Where it strains |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Location-adjusted** | "Equal local purchasing power" | Lowest cost; tracks local markets | Pay cuts on relocation have produced documented attrition and morale damage elsewhere; can feel like a penalty for moving; administratively complex |
| **National/regional bands** | "Same country, same pay" | Simpler; defensible; contains cost | Hard edges at borders; pressure from high-cost cities within a country |
| **Global role-based bands** | "Same work, same pay, anywhere" | Cleanest story; powerful for scarce skills | Highest headline cost; risks distortion against local markets in both directions |

Two constraints belong on the table from the start: several jurisdictions restrict reducing pay upon relocation or require consent for contractual changes, so any option must be modeled country by country; and retroactive harm should be ruled out entirely — no one should lose pay for a move already made in good faith. We would gently suggest that leadership take this decision at the Month 3–4 decision point, with finance modeling all three options in full, and that whichever story is chosen, its logic be published. People forgive a philosophy they disagree with more readily than one they cannot see.

## 9. Managers: The Transmission Layer

Every layer above ultimately travels through a manager — including the plant supervisor and the store manager, whose charters matter as much as any product team's. We would propose investing accordingly: training in outcome-based goal-setting, charter facilitation, fair scheduling, and cross-cultural feedback (direct in Amsterdam reads as blunt in Tokyo; indirect in Tokyo reads as evasive in Amsterdam). Manager capability is the single highest-leverage line item in this entire framework.

## 10. The Business Case, in Brief

Finance colleagues will rightly ask for the arithmetic, so we offer its shape — directional figures, to be replaced by properly modeled numbers at the Month 3–4 decision point:

- **Footprint:** office cost per desk commonly runs to several thousand dollars annually in major markets; a considered 20–30% footprint reduction in a company of this size frees resources on a scale that funds the gathering rhythm, stipends, and manager training several times over — with the remainder returned to the business.
- **Attrition:** replacing an employee is commonly estimated at half to twice annual salary depending on seniority, and flexibility consistently ranks among the top stated reasons people stay or leave. A single-point improvement in regretted attrition, across tens of thousands of employees, plausibly pays for the program.
- **Frontline predictability:** stable-scheduling experiments in retail associate predictable rosters with measurable sales and productivity gains — the cheapest retention lever in this document.
- **The honest caveat:** these are directional claims, not a budget. We would propose that the Days 1–60 phase produce the real model, so the group decides on evidence rather than on our arithmetic.

## 11. Suggested Roadmap

**Days 1–60 — Listen and map** *(program lead + regional HR; works councils engaged at kickoff)*
